title: Digital Money and Fintech
summary: How money became data: how card and phone payments work behind the scenes, how app banks and open banking use technology, how payments are secured, how to spot scams and avoid becoming a money mule, what cryptocurrency and blockchain really are, and how AI and data are shaping the future of money.
learn: How card, contactless and phone payments work behind the scenes
How fintech, app-based banking and open banking use technology
How encryption, tokenisation and authentication keep payments secure
How to recognise payment scams and why being a money mule is a crime
What cryptocurrency and blockchain are, and their benefits and risks
How AI and data are changing money, and the issues this raises
intro: Most money today isn't coins or notes: it's data moving between computers. Tap your phone and in under a second messages zip between banks, card networks and fraud-detecting AI. In this topic you'll find out what happens when you pay contactless, how app-based banks and fintech companies work, how payments are kept secure, how criminals try to trick young people out of their money (or into moving it for them), what cryptocurrency and blockchain really are, and you'll design a fintech app of your own.

pages.title: Tap to pay
pages.spec: Describe how card, contactless and mobile payments work and the systems involved
pages.summary: When you pay by card or phone, a chain of computer systems checks the payment in about a second: the terminal, the shop's bank, the card network and your bank. Contactless uses NFC radio, and phone wallets use tokens instead of your real card number. Fewer than one in ten UK payments now use cash.
pages.starter: When did you last pay with cash? How did you pay for the last thing you bought?
sc: I can describe how payments have changed
I can describe the steps in a card payment
I can explain how contactless and phone payments work

Cash is now used for only a small share of UK payments
Contactless cards, phones and watches are the most common ways to pay in shops
Bank transfers are almost instant with Faster Payments
Terminal reads the card or phone using NFC
Request goes to the shop's bank, then the card network (Visa, Mastercard)
Your bank checks: enough money? Looks like fraud?
Approved or declined, all in about a second
Apple Pay and Google Pay store a token, not your real card number
You unlock with fingerprint, face or PIN
Each payment uses a one-time code
Safer than a physical card if your phone is stolen

blocks.text: Money as data

Today, most money exists as numbers in banks' computer systems. In the UK, cash is now used for only a small share of payments, while contactless cards, phones and smartwatches have become the most common way to pay in shops. Bank transfers using the UK's Faster Payments system usually arrive within seconds.
What happens when you pay

blocks.title: Following a contactless payment
blocks.context: You tap your card to buy lunch for £4.50.
steps: The terminal reads your card using radio waves and asks the shop's bank to process it.
The shop's bank sends the request through the **[[card network]]** (such as Visa or Mastercard).
The card network passes it to your bank, which checks your balance and runs fraud checks.
Your bank sends back "approved" (this is **[[authorisation]]**), and the terminal beeps.
blocks.answer: Four organisations' computers have exchanged messages in about one second. The money actually moves between banks later, often the next day (called settlement).

blocks.text: Contactless and NFC

**[[contactless|Contactless]]** payment uses **[[NFC]]** (near-field communication), a type of short-range radio that only works within a few centimetres. Shops often accept contactless card payments up to £100 without a PIN, though banks sometimes ask for the PIN to check it's really you.
Digital wallets

A **[[digital wallet]]** such as Apple Pay or Google Pay stores payment cards on a phone or watch. Instead of your real card number, it stores a token (a substitute number), and every payment uses a one-time code. You unlock it with your fingerprint, face or PIN, so a stolen phone is harder to use than a stolen card.

blocks.caption: Ways to pay
head: Method
How it works
Security
rows: Card chip creates a unique code; you enter a PIN
NFC radio; no PIN for smaller amounts
NFC plus a token instead of the card number
Banking app login, confirmation of payee
Can be lost or stolen, but private

steps: Each person takes a role: customer, terminal, shop's bank, card network, customer's bank.
Pass a "payment message" card along the chain, adding the information each role checks.
Run three scenarios: a normal payment, not enough money, and a suspicious payment from another country.
Draw a diagram of the payment chain.

q.q: What does the customer's bank check before approving a payment?
q.a: That the card is valid and not reported lost, there's enough money or credit, and that the payment doesn't look like fraud (unusual place, amount or pattern).

q.q: What happened in the suspicious payment scenario?
q.a: The customer's bank's fraud system flagged it as unusual and declined it, or asked the customer to confirm it in their banking app.

pages.title: Fintech and app banking
pages.spec: Explain what fintech is and how app-based banks, open banking and APIs are changing financial services
pages.summary: Fintech (financial technology) uses software to provide financial services. App-based banks offer instant notifications, budgeting tools and quick account opening. Open banking lets you securely share your bank data with other apps using APIs. Fintech brings convenience but also risks such as easy credit like Buy Now, Pay Later.
pages.starter: What can you do on a banking app that you couldn't do in a bank branch?
sc: I can explain what fintech is and give examples
I can explain open banking and the role of APIs
I can evaluate fintech products such as Buy Now, Pay Later

b: Fintech = financial technology
App-based banks, payment apps, budgeting apps, money transfer apps
The UK, and London in particular, is one of the world's biggest fintech hubs
Northern Ireland has a growing fintech and financial software industry
An API lets one program request data or services from another
Open banking: you can let approved apps access your bank data securely
e.g. a budgeting app shows all your accounts in one place
You give consent and can withdraw it at any time
BNPL lets you split payments, often with no interest if paid on time
Easy to use: one click at checkout
Risk: building up debt across several purchases
Missed payments can lead to fees and harm your credit record

blocks.text: What is fintech?

**[[fintech|Fintech]]** (financial technology) means using software and technology to provide financial services. It includes app-based banks (such as Monzo, Starling and Revolut), payment apps, budgeting tools, money transfer services and investing apps. The UK is one of the world's biggest fintech centres, and Belfast has a growing financial technology sector too.

blocks.title: Features of app-based banking
items: Open an account in minutes using your phone and ID
Freeze your card instantly in the app if it's lost

blocks.text: Open banking and APIs

An **[[API]]** (application programming interface) is a set of rules that lets one program request data or services from another. **[[open banking|Open banking]]**, introduced in the UK in 2018, requires big banks to let customers securely share their account data with approved apps through APIs, but only with the customer's consent.

blocks.caption: Open banking examples
head: Use
How it helps
rows: See all your accounts in one place and track spending
A lender checks your real income and spending to decide on a loan
Pay directly from your bank at checkout without a card
Apps that move small amounts into savings automatically

blocks.text: Regulation

Financial services are tightly **[[regulation|regulated]]**. In the UK, the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) makes sure firms treat customers fairly and keep money safe. Money in UK banks is protected up to a limit by the Financial Services Compensation Scheme (FSCS) if a bank fails. Always check a financial company is authorised by the FCA.
Buy Now, Pay Later

**[[Buy Now Pay Later|Buy Now, Pay Later]]** (BNPL) lets shoppers split a purchase into several payments, often with no interest if paid on time. It's quick and convenient, but it's still borrowing. Using several BNPL plans at once can lead to debt, and missed payments can lead to charges, debt collection and a damaged credit record. New UK rules are bringing BNPL under FCA regulation.
Be wary of anything that makes spending or borrowing feel effortless. If you can't afford something now, think carefully about whether you'll be able to afford the payments later.

blocks.title: Fintech review
steps: Look at the screenshots of three (fictional) fintech apps: a teen banking app, a budgeting app using open banking, and a BNPL checkout.
For each, list two features that help users and one risk.

q.a: The teen banking app with parental controls: instant notifications and savings pots help build good habits, and it doesn't offer credit.

q.q: What should you ask before connecting your bank account to an app?
q.a: E.g. "Is this company authorised by the FCA? What data will it access, how long will it keep it, and how do I remove access?"

Sharing your bank data securely with approved apps, with your consent

practice.a: Benefits, e.g. spreads cost, often no interest (1-2); risks, e.g. debt, fees, credit record, encourages impulse buying (1-2); conclusion (1). Max 4.

pages.title: Securing payments
pages.spec: Explain how encryption, tokenisation, strong authentication and AI fraud detection protect digital payments
pages.summary: Digital payments are protected by several layers: encryption scrambles data in transit, tokenisation replaces card numbers, strong customer authentication requires two different types of proof, and AI systems analyse every payment in real time to spot fraud.
pages.starter: What stops someone who finds your card number online from spending your money?
sc: I can explain how encryption and tokenisation protect payment data
I can explain strong customer authentication
I can describe how AI detects fraud

b: Encryption: scrambles data so only the right system can read it
HTTPS and the padlock protect card details sent to websites
Tokenisation: a substitute number replaces the real card number
A stolen token is useless elsewhere
Strong customer authentication needs two of three types of proof
Something you know: PIN or password
Something you have: phone or card
Something you are: fingerprint or face (biometrics)
AI checks every payment in milliseconds
Looks for unusual amounts, places, times or devices
Can block payments or ask you to confirm in your app
False positives: sometimes genuine payments get blocked

blocks.text: Encryption and tokenisation

**[[encryption|Encryption]]** scrambles data so that only someone with the right key can read it. When you enter card details on a website, HTTPS encryption (shown by the padlock) protects them as they travel. Card chips also use encryption to create a unique code for every payment, so copying one payment's data doesn't let a criminal make another.

**[[tokenisation|Tokenisation]]** replaces the real card number with a substitute number (a token). Phone wallets and many online shops store tokens instead of real card numbers, so if a criminal steals a token, it's useless anywhere else.
Strong customer authentication
UK rules require **[[strong customer authentication]]** (SCA) for many online payments: you must prove who you are using two different types of evidence.

blocks.caption: Types of authentication
head: Type
Examples
rows: Your phone (receiving a code or approving in an app), your card

blocks.text: Two of the same type (like a password and a memorable word) don't count, because one stolen notebook could reveal both.
AI fraud detection

**[[fraud detection|Fraud detection]]** systems use AI to analyse every payment in milliseconds. They learn what's normal for each customer and look for warning signs: a large payment from a new device, a purchase in another country an hour after one at home, or lots of small payments very quickly. Suspicious payments can be blocked or the customer asked to confirm.

blocks.caption: Is it fraud?
head: Payment
Likely AI decision
rows: £1,200 from a new phone in another country at 3am
Ten £1 payments to the same website in a minute
£40 in a shop the customer often uses

blocks.text: AI isn't perfect. A false positive blocks a genuine payment (annoying on holiday!), while a false negative lets fraud through. Banks tune their systems to balance the two.

blocks.title: Be the fraud AI
steps: Read the spending profile of "Erin", 15, who lives in Enniskillen.
For 12 new payments, decide: approve, ask Erin to confirm, or block.
Write three rules your fraud AI follows.
Compare with another pair: where did you disagree and why?

q.a: E.g. IF payment is over 5 times Erin's usual largest payment THEN ask to confirm; IF payment is in another country within 2 hours of one in Enniskillen THEN block; IF more than 5 payments to one site in a minute THEN block.

q.q: Give an example where your rules would make a false positive.
q.a: E.g. Erin buys a £150 concert ticket for her birthday, much bigger than usual, so it's flagged even though it's genuine.

o: Scrambles data so only the right system can read it
Replacing a card number with a substitute number

check.q: Which pair counts as strong customer authentication?
o: A password and a code sent to your phone
A password and a memorable word

check.q: What might AI fraud detection do with an unusual payment?
o: Block it or ask you to confirm

practice.q: Explain strong customer authentication, with an example.
practice.a: Two different types of proof (1) from know/have/are (1); e.g. password plus fingerprint/code on phone (1).

practice.q: Describe how AI helps detect payment fraud.
practice.a: Learns normal behaviour for each customer (1); checks each payment in real time for unusual patterns (1); blocks or asks for confirmation (1).

pages.title: Scams and money mules
pages.spec: Recognise common payment scams, explain why money muling is a crime, and describe how to protect yourself
pages.summary: Criminals use phishing, fake websites, impersonation and social media to trick people into sending money or details. Young people are often targeted to become money mules, letting criminals move stolen money through their accounts, which is a serious crime. Stopping, checking and talking to a trusted adult is the best defence.
pages.starter: You see a post: "Earn £500 this week! Just let us use your bank account." What questions should you ask?
sc: I can recognise common scam techniques
I can explain what a money mule is and the consequences
I can describe how to protect myself and where to get help

b: Phishing (email), smishing (text) and fake websites
Impersonation: pretending to be your bank, the police or a delivery firm
Urgency and pressure: "act now or lose your money"
Too good to be true: fake prizes, investments, cheap tickets
Criminals ask young people to receive and pass on money "for a fee"
Advertised as easy cash, jobs or "favours" on social media
The money comes from crime such as fraud or drugs
It's money laundering: accounts closed, possible prison, hard to get a phone contract or student loan
Stop: take a moment before sharing details or sending money
Challenge: could it be fake? It's OK to say no
Protect: contact your bank directly; tell a trusted adult
Call 159 to reach your bank safely if you think you've been scammed

blocks.text: Scam techniques
Scammers use **[[social engineering]]**: manipulating people rather than hacking computers.

blocks.caption: Common scams
head: Scam
How it works
Warning signs
rows: Emails or texts with links to fake login pages
Urgent tone, odd sender address, link doesn't match the real site
Pretending to be your bank, the police or HMRC
Asking you to move money to a "safe account" (banks never do this)
Cheap trainers, tickets or games that never arrive
Prices too good to be true; payment by bank transfer only
Fake offers of free skins or in-game currency
Asking for your login or a payment first
Celebrity endorsements, pressure to act now

blocks.text: **[[authorised push payment fraud|Authorised push payment (APP) fraud]]** is when someone is tricked into sending money to a criminal themselves. Since October 2024, UK payment firms must reimburse most victims of APP fraud (up to £85,000), but it's still far better not to be scammed in the first place.
Money mules

A **[[money mule]]** is someone who lets criminals use their bank account to receive and move stolen money. Criminals often target teenagers and students on social media, offering "easy money" or a "job" that just involves receiving and passing on payments.

Being a money mule is money laundering, a serious crime, even if you didn't know where the money came from. Consequences can include your bank account being closed, a fraud marker that makes it hard to get a bank account, phone contract, student loan or mortgage for years, and a possible prison sentence.
Protect yourself

blocks.title: Staying safe with money online
items: Never share your PIN, passwords or one-time codes, even with someone claiming to be from your bank
Your bank will never ask you to move money to a "safe account"
Check websites carefully and use secure payment methods (cards or PayPal give more protection than bank transfers)
If an offer seems too good to be true, it probably is
Call 159 to reach your bank safely; report scams to Action Fraud or the PSNI
Tell a trusted adult straight away if something feels wrong

blocks.title: Scam spotter
steps: Look at the eight (fictional) messages and adverts, including a parcel text, a "job" advert on social media and a cheap concert ticket.
Decide which are scams and highlight the warning signs.
For the "job" advert, explain why it's money muling and what could happen to someone who agrees.
Write a short warning post for younger pupils.

q.q: What warning signs are in the "job" advert?
q.a: Easy money for little work; asks to use your bank account; contact only through social media; urgency ("start today"); vague about the company.

q.q: What should you do if you've already shared your bank details?
q.a: Tell a trusted adult immediately, call your bank on 159 or the number on your card, change passwords, and report it to Action Fraud or the PSNI.

o: Someone who lets criminals move money through their account

check.q: Will your bank ever ask you to move money to a "safe account"?
What number can you call to reach your bank safely in the UK?

o: Manipulating people into giving information or money

practice.q: Describe three warning signs of a payment scam.
practice.a: Any three: urgency/pressure (1); too good to be true (1); asks for PIN/codes/passwords (1); asks to move money to a safe account (1); unusual sender/link (1); bank transfer only (1).

practice.q: Explain why being a money mule is dangerous for a young person.
practice.a: It's a crime: money laundering (1); possible prosecution/prison (1); bank account closed/fraud marker affecting future loans, phone contracts, etc. (1).

pages.title: Crypto and blockchain
pages.spec: Explain what blockchain and cryptocurrency are, and evaluate their benefits and risks
pages.summary: A blockchain is a shared, tamper-resistant digital record (ledger) stored on many computers. Cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin use blockchains to record transactions without a bank. Crypto is very volatile, often used in scams, and some types use huge amounts of energy. Central banks are exploring their own digital currencies.
pages.starter: If there's no bank, who keeps track of who owns what money?
sc: I can explain what a blockchain is
I can explain how cryptocurrency works and how it differs from normal money
I can evaluate the risks of cryptocurrency

b: A ledger is a record of transactions
A blockchain is a ledger shared across many computers
Transactions are grouped into blocks, linked using cryptographic hashes
Changing an old block would break the chain, so tampering is easy to spot
Digital currency recorded on a blockchain, with no central bank
Bitcoin (2009) was the first; thousands now exist
New blocks are added by mining (proof of work) or staking (proof of stake)
Stablecoins are linked to normal money like the US dollar
Very volatile: prices can halve in weeks
Not protected like bank savings; lost keys mean lost money
Widely used in scams, hacks and crime
Proof-of-work mining uses huge amounts of electricity

blocks.text: Ledgers and blockchains

A **[[ledger]]** is a record of who has paid whom. Normally, banks keep ledgers. A **[[blockchain]]** is a ledger copied across thousands of computers. Transactions are grouped into blocks, and each block contains a cryptographic hash (a digital fingerprint) of the previous block, linking them into a chain. If anyone changes an old transaction, its hash changes and the chain no longer matches, so tampering is obvious.

blocks.title: Why tampering breaks the chain
blocks.context: Block 2 stores the fingerprint of block 1. Block 3 stores the fingerprint of block 2.
steps: A cheat changes a payment in block 1.
Block 1's fingerprint changes, so it no longer matches the one stored in block 2.
To hide it, the cheat would have to redo every later block, on most of the thousands of computers at once.
blocks.answer: That's practically impossible, which is why blockchains are described as tamper-resistant.

blocks.text: Cryptocurrency
A **[[cryptocurrency]]** is digital money recorded on a blockchain rather than by a bank. Bitcoin, launched in 2009, was the first; there are now thousands.

blocks.caption: Bank money vs cryptocurrency
head: Feature
Bank money (pounds)
Cryptocurrency
rows: Banks, overseen by the Bank of England
Savings protected up to a limit (FSCS)
Usually no protection; lost keys mean lost money

blocks.text: A **[[stablecoin]]** is a cryptocurrency designed to keep a steady value by linking it to normal money, such as the US dollar. The UK is introducing rules for stablecoins and other crypto.
Energy and risks

Bitcoin uses "proof of work" mining, where computers compete to solve puzzles, using as much electricity as some entire countries. Ethereum switched to "proof of stake" in 2022, cutting its energy use by over 99%. Crypto is also widely used in scams: fake investment schemes, hacked exchanges and "rug pulls" where creators vanish with investors' money.

Blockchains are also used outside crypto: tracking food and medicine supply chains, recording certificates and managing digital ownership. But many projects have found a normal database works just as well.
Central bank digital currencies

A **[[CBDC]]** (central bank digital currency) is digital money issued by a central bank. The Bank of England has been exploring a possible "digital pound", but hasn't decided whether to introduce one. Supporters say it could make payments cheaper and more resilient; critics worry about privacy and government control over how money is spent.

blocks.title: Build a paper blockchain
steps: Each group starts a ledger of class "tokens". Each block (an index card) records 3 transactions and the "fingerprint" of the previous block (use the simple hash your teacher gives you, e.g. add up all the numbers in the block).
Every group keeps a copy of every block.
One pupil secretly changes a transaction in an early block. Can the class find it?
Discuss: what are the strengths and weaknesses of this system compared with a bank?

q.q: How did the class spot the changed transaction?
q.a: The changed block's fingerprint no longer matched the fingerprint stored in the next block, and it didn't match the copies other groups held.

q.q: Give one strength and one weakness of the blockchain compared with a bank.
q.a: Strength: no single organisation controls it and tampering is easy to spot. Weakness: slow, everyone has to store copies, and mistakes can't be easily reversed.

o: A shared, tamper-resistant digital ledger stored on many computers

check.q: What does volatile mean for a cryptocurrency?
o: Its price can change a lot very quickly
A cryptocurrency linked to normal money to keep a steady value
check.why: e.g. linked to the US dollar.

practice.q: Explain why a blockchain is described as tamper-resistant.
practice.a: Each block stores the hash/fingerprint of the previous block (1); changing a block changes its hash so the chain no longer matches (1); copies on many computers would also need changing (1).

practice.q: Discuss whether young people should invest in cryptocurrency.
practice.a: Possible gains/new technology (1); volatility, scams, no protection, irreversible (1-2); regulation and energy issues (1); conclusion (1). Max 4.

pages.title: The future of money
pages.spec: Evaluate the use of AI and data in finance and the move towards a cashless society, and design a responsible fintech solution
pages.summary: AI is used in finance for credit decisions, fraud detection, customer chatbots and trading. This raises concerns about bias and fairness. As cash use falls, there are debates about a cashless society and financial inclusion. Responsible fintech design puts users' wellbeing, security and inclusion first.
pages.starter: Should a computer decide whether someone gets a loan? What information should it be allowed to use?
sc: I can describe how AI and data are used in finance
I can discuss the impacts of a cashless society
I can design a responsible fintech app

b: Credit scoring: AI helps decide who gets loans and phones on contract
Fraud detection and security checks
Chatbots answer customer questions
AI trading systems buy and sell shares in milliseconds
AI learns from past data, which may reflect past unfairness
Algorithmic bias could treat some groups unfairly
People have a right to an explanation of important automated decisions
Regulators expect firms to check AI for fairness
Card and phone payments are fast and convenient
But some people rely on cash: older people, people in rural areas, people budgeting carefully
Cash still works in a power cut or system outage

blocks.text: AI in finance

blocks.caption: How AI is used in finance
head: Use
What AI does
rows: Predicts whether someone is likely to repay a loan
Spots unusual payments in real time
Chatbots answer questions and help with problems
Algorithms buy and sell shares in fractions of a second
Apps predict your spending and suggest savings

blocks.text: A **[[credit score]]** is a number lenders use to judge how likely you are to repay money you borrow. It's based on your history of borrowing and paying bills. AI is increasingly used to make these decisions.
Fairness and bias

**[[algorithmic bias|Algorithmic bias]]** happens when an AI system treats some groups unfairly, often because it learned from data that reflected past unfairness. For example, an AI could give lower credit limits to people from certain areas even if they're just as likely to repay. UK data protection law gives people rights when important decisions are made about them automatically, including the right to have a human review the decision.
A cashless society?
In a **[[cashless society]]**, all payments would be digital. Cash use in the UK has fallen sharply, and some shops no longer accept it.

blocks.caption: Weighing up a cashless society
head: For
Against
rows: Excludes people without bank accounts or smartphones
Cash works during power cuts and system outages
Easier to track spending and taxes
Less privacy: every payment leaves a record
Some people budget better with physical cash

blocks.text: **[[financial inclusion|Financial inclusion]]** means everyone having access to useful, affordable financial services. UK law now requires access to cash to be protected, including banking hubs in towns that have lost their bank branches.
Designing responsible fintech

blocks.title: Principles for responsible fintech
items: Wellbeing: help people save and avoid debt, don't push spending
Security: strong authentication, encryption, fraud protection
Privacy: collect only the data needed; be clear about how it's used
Inclusion: accessible design; options for people with less money or confidence
Fairness: test AI for bias; explain decisions

q.q: How does your app protect users' security and wellbeing?
q.a: Fingerprint/PIN login and notifications for every payment; no credit or BNPL; parental controls; no adverts or "deals" that encourage spending; clear privacy settings.
